item.title: Hulu’s Best Comedy Is Coming Back This Winter, So Now’s The Time to Resubscribe
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Waiting for ‘Only Murders in the Building’ Season 6? Find out when it’s coming back to Hulu, casting details, and more.
item.content:encoded:
“Only Murders in the Building” Season 6 is headed to London

After months of tantalizing cast announcements, we finally have a premiere date for the sixth season of Hulu’s murder-mystery comedy, “Only Murders in the Building.”

The show is coming back to Hulu on December 8, 2026. Like previous seasons, episodes will air weekly, giving fans time to theorize their own solutions to this season’s murder.

Want to know more about the latest mystery? Read on for all the details we know so far about Season 6. Fair warning: We’re going to discuss spoilers from Season 5!

Keep up with all the latest in entertainment news

Subscribe to CableTV.com's email newsletter for the latest TV event viewing guides, entertaining takes, and money-saving promotions.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

A trip to the other side of the pond

For the past five seasons, Charles, Oliver, and Mabel have mostly stuck to the name of their own podcast. They only cover murders that happened in the building. But this season, the murder stretches that definition just a little bit: Cinda Canning died right at the edge of The Arconia’s property. She seemingly dragged her body up to the building’s entrance and used her dying breath to place her hand on the gate.

So Cinda’s death is officially our heroes’ problem. But Cinda’s murder likely didn’t start in New York City. She was investigating a murder overseas in England, so the gang will travel there to figure out what exactly happened to their former idol. According to Variety, the show will even be temporarily retitled “Only Murders in London.” It’s giving “Schmicago,” guys.Luckily for us viewers, a new locale means a ton of British celebrity cameos. Even better, a whole bunch of those cameos will be “Doctor Who” stars. (David Tennant, Peter Capaldi, and Jodie Whittaker have all played The Doctor in the last twenty years.)

What do you think the overlap is on people who watched both “Wizards of Waverly Place” (Selena Gomez’s Disney Channel show) and “Doctor Who” growing up in the 2000s? They’re both family-friendly genre TV with low-budget special effects, so probably pretty big, right? I feel like this is going to be one popular crossover.

Here are all of the British actor cameos that we know about right now:

  • David Tennant
  • Peter Capaldi
  • Jodie Whittaker
  • Nicola Coughlan
  • Martin Freeman
  • Olivia Colman
  • Jim Broadbent
  • Lesley Nicol
  • Richard Ayoade
  • Adrian Lukis
  • Kathryn Hunter
  • Jennifer Saunders
  • Sean Teale
  • Simone Ashley
  • Amar Chadha-Patel
  • Rhea Norwood
  • Matthew Beard
  • Sharon Horgan
  • Geri Halliwell-Horner
  • Jamie Demetriou
  • Anjana Vasan
  • Jane Horrocks
  • Derek Jacobi
It makes you wonder how exactly they plan on squeezing so many cameos into just one season (and how many on this list, keeping with tradition, will play themselves). And will Paul Rudd come back yet again, using another ridiculous accent?

We’ll only know when the series returns to Hulu on December 8. Until then, I’ll be reorganizing my murder board.

Where to watch “Only Murders”

Hulu

Hulu is home to a lot of award-winning shows, from comedies like “Only Murders in the Building” to dramas pretending to be comedies like “The Bear.” But it’s best enjoyed through the Hulu on Disney+ portal, available exclusively to Disney Bundle subscribers.

item.title: Live Sports Playbook: What US Fans Pay to Watch in 2026
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: U.S. sports fans spend an average of $65.92 a month on live TV services, yet blackouts, buffering, and broadcast delays still disrupt viewing.
item.content:encoded:
Sports fans pay for TV but still face uncertainty

Being a sports fan in 2026 can feel like a part-time job. One league might be relatively simple to follow, while another can send you bouncing between a live TV service, standalone streaming apps, and league-specific packages. Even sticking with a traditional TV provider doesn’t necessarily get you out of the maze. That fragmentation shows up clearly in CableTV.com’s 2026 live sports viewing survey. U.S. sports fans use an average of 2.4 paid TV or streaming services to watch sports. Even with multiple subscriptions, many still deal with blackouts, buffering, and uncertainty over whether their setup will carry the game or event they want. Our findings show the cost of watching live sports in 2026 and where that investment falls short. In this report, we’ll follow that experience from paying the monthly bill to figuring out where to watch and navigating the issues that can disrupt game day on TV. We also explore how fans adapt and what could ultimately push them to switch providers.

By the numbers

The monthly bill tells only part of the story. These four findings highlight what fans are paying, where the viewing experience falls short, and what could push them to change their setup.

  • $65.92 average monthly spend on live TV services for sports
  • $56.58 average maximum fans would pay per month for live sports alone
  • 66.7% would switch providers to save $20 a month
  • 47.0% experienced buffering during a critical game-time moment

How much are fans paying to watch live sports?

Let’s start with the bill. U.S. sports fans spend an average of $65.92 per month on the cable, satellite, or live TV streaming services they use to watch sports, with a median monthly spend of $63.00. Asked separately what they would pay strictly for live sports coverage, respondents set a lower average ceiling of $56.58 per month. The questions measure slightly different things, but the contrast is still revealing. Fans’ broader TV spending for sports access runs more than $9.00 higher than the maximum they say they would pay for live sports alone.

Most fans juggle multiple services

That $65.92 figure is only part of the picture, especially when you consider how many services fans use to watch sports. Survey respondents use an average of 2.4 paid TV or streaming services for sports, with two services being the most common response at 30.9%. Only 25.8% use just one paid service, meaning nearly three out of four fans use at least two. Services such as Amazon Prime Video, ESPN Select (ESPN+), and Peacock carry exclusive games and events that may not be available through a fan’s primary live TV provider. For some fans, those subscriptions aren’t extras; they’re part of completing the lineup.

Live sports keep viewers subscribed — but loyalty has limits

Sports fans don’t get much say in where their favorite teams, leagues, or competitions end up on TV. As viewers chase coverage from one platform to the next, provider loyalty can feel fluid. The loyalty stays with the team; the subscription follows the rights. That dynamic shows up clearly in our survey. More than half of respondents (54.9%) say live sports is the only reason they still pay for a TV provider or live streaming service, and 57.9% pay for at least one service only during a specific sports season. Taken together, those findings suggest that sports subscriptions can function less like year-round commitments and more like tickets to the games fans care about. That loyalty has limits, too. Nearly half (46.4%) would cancel their TV service entirely if their team’s games were available elsewhere, but canceling isn’t always as clean as it sounds. Nearly 46% of fans have kept paying for a service they meant to cancel after a season ended. A service can feel essential while the games are on and easy to question once the season ends.

Fans want more flexible ways to pay

Price makes those limits even clearer. Two-thirds of fans (66.7%) would switch providers to save $20 a month, while 56.5% say they would stop paying to watch a league they like if prices rose again. But many are open to compromises instead: About 63% of fans would accept more commercials for a cheaper sports package, and 52.2% would pay for access to only one team’s games if that option existed.Some fans already use more flexible payment options. In the past year, 41.7% have bought a single-game TV pass or pay-per-view event, while 40.7% say they’d prefer paying per game or event over a monthly subscription. Live TV streaming providers are testing more targeted options, too. YouTube TV now offers a Sports Plan alongside other genre-based plans, while Sling TV sells one-, three-, and seven-day passes. One gives viewers more control over what they subscribe to; the other gives them more control over how long they keep it.

Finding the game is still harder than it should be

Paying for the game is one thing. Finding it is another. U.S. sports fans spend about 12 minutes each week figuring out where live games or events are airing — not a huge amount of time on its own, but still a recurring chore for something viewers are already paying to watch. Knowing where to look doesn’t always guarantee access, either. Only 21.7% of respondents say they’re extremely confident that their main TV setup will carry any given game they want to watch.

Only 21.7% of sports fans

believe their current TV setup will get them the game.

Blackouts make that uncertainty more than an inconvenience. In the past year, 37.7% of fans say a blackout prevented them from watching a local team, while 26.0% say they can’t watch their in-market team at all with their current setup. Nearly half (45.8%) have even considered switching providers specifically to get access to a regional sports network.

Fans want the game before the extras

When fans choose a service for live sports, getting the games they care about matters most. Access to favorite teams, leagues, or events ranked as the most important factor in our survey, followed closely by price and then picture quality and technical reliability. Convenience and viewing features rank much lower. Ease of use ranked fifth overall, while multiview and other viewing features finished last. Before fans worry about bells and whistles, they want to know one thing: Will this service actually carry what I want to watch?

What matters most when choosing a sports TV service?

Rank Factor Average rank
1 Access to favorite teams, leagues, or events 2.69
2 Price 2.84
3 Picture quality and reliability 3.11
4 No blackouts or local-market restrictions 3.67
5 Ease of use 4.11
6 Multiview and other viewing features 4.59

Lower average rank means respondents considered the factor more important.

A premium price doesn’t guarantee a premium viewing experience

After fans piece together the right services and track down the game, the stream still has to keep up with the action. Nearly half (47.0%) say they’ve experienced buffering during a critical moment in the past year. Being behind the action creates another frustration. More than a third of fans (35.8%) say stream lag has caused problems, while 36.7% have had a phone notification or social post spoil a play before they saw it. For live sports, even getting the game isn’t quite enough if another screen gives away the moment first. Even so, fans are investing in the viewing experience. About 43.0% have upgraded their TV or internet service specifically for sports. At the same time, 33.2% say streaming looks worse than cable or satellite TV for fast-moving action.

How much streaming delay will fans tolerate?

For live sports, the word “live” sets a high bar. Just over half of our survey respondents (50.6%) say they’ll accept no more than 10 seconds of delay from the actual action, including 16.1% who won’t tolerate any delay at all. Another 20.6% consider 11 to 30 seconds acceptable, but tolerance drops from there. Only 5.7% say more than a minute is acceptable, while 4.2% say delay doesn’t matter to them. That low tolerance is a tricky fit for the streaming era. According to Stats Perform, major streaming feeds during Super Bowl LX ran 48 to 62 seconds behind the field, compared with 38 seconds for cable and 19 seconds for over-the-air TV.

How sports fans work around cost and access problems

When the standard setup falls short, fans improvise. Some change when they subscribe, some change where they watch, and others find another route to the game. As noted earlier, 57.9% pay for at least one service only during a specific sports season, allowing their subscription lineup to shift with the calendar. Blackouts can send viewers outside their usual setup altogether. About 40.3% have gone to a bar or someone else’s home because a game was blacked out, while 23.1% have used a VPN or similar workaround to get past one. Separately, 25.8% report watching an unauthorized stream in the past year, though the survey doesn’t say what motivated them.

Free TV still has a place in the lineup

Not every alternative comes with another monthly bill. Nearly one-third of sports fans (32.5%) say they own and use an over-the-air antenna for sports. When games air on local broadcast channels, an antenna can complement a paid TV or streaming setup rather than replace it. That mix of old and new technology captures where sports viewing stands in 2026. Fans are changing when they subscribe, where they watch, and what they add to their setups to keep up with the games they care about. The rights may determine where the games live, but fans are finding their own ways to get there.

Methodology

To compile our findings, CableTV.com surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults who said they watch live sports on TV or online. The survey was conducted via Pollfish on August 6, 2026, and the results were post-stratified to reflect the broader U.S. population on key demographics. Responses were self-reported. Monthly spending and willingness-to-pay amounts were collected in price ranges, so the reported dollar figures are estimates based on values assigned to those ranges rather than respondents’ individual bills.

item.title: Disney+ Adds Free Live College Football — Here’s How to Watch for Less
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Disney+ now includes select live ESPN college football games at no extra cost. See how this new streaming perk works and how to stack current deals for max savings.
item.content:encoded:
You can score live college football games on Disney+ this fall

Even if you’re not the type to spend your fall weekends glued to football games, having free access to some big matches isn’t a perk to turn your nose up at. ESPN announced yesterday that Disney+ will stream select college football games every Saturday this fall. This is a totally free bonus for Disney+ subscribers, giving them big ESPN and ABC matchups within their existing Disney+ app, no pricey add-ons or extra channels needed. Disney teased this earlier this month, announcing that a main part of its current strategy is to increase live sports content. I don’t get excited for college sports ’til basketball starts (I’m a UNC alum, can you blame me for skipping over football season?), so to check the consensus on this deal among die-hard college football fans, I dove into some Reddit threads. Word on the r/CFB streets is that while real fans likely already have ESPN access, this is a killer freebie for casual Disney+ subscribers. Plus, as a few users pointed out, having live games on Disney+ is a handy backup option if carriage disputes ever temporarily black out regular live TV services like YouTube TV (again). Keep reading for more details on how this new streaming perk works, plus how you can stack it with existing discounts to pay even less.

Pair live sports with Disney+’s best streaming discounts

While standard Disney+ subscribers get these bonus games at no extra cost, you can stretch your buck even further by bundling. Folks who want full access to live sports, original series, and game replays should opt for the discounted Trio bundle, which includes Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Select. And real sportsballs should upgrade to the Disney+ bundle with ESPN Unlimited — but then you wouldn’t even need these free games, since ESPN Unlimited includes live linear feeds of ESPN’s entire family of networks! If you’re currently a college student, you can save even more. The brand-new Disney+ and Hulu student bundle knocks 50% off the regular (already discounted) bundle price, giving students both services for just $6.49 a month. item.title: RedZone During US Open a ‘Major Step Forward’ for Tennis Fans, McEnroe Says
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: The U.S. Open Tennis Championships will take a page from the NFL with its RedZone coverage on ESPN during the early rounds of the tournament.
item.content:encoded:
ESPN introduces whip-around show for U.S. Open Tennis Championships

Professional tennis has, at times, struggled to hold onto viewers due to the sheer length of matches. But during this year’s U.S. Open Tennis Championships, ESPN is unveiling a potential solution: the sport’s very own RedZone.

Starting August 30, the first day of the tournament, tennis fans can watch “RedZone at the U.S. Open” — a whiparound show featuring live look-ins of every match, every day, through September 4. The show is available only to ESPN Unlimited subscribers.

The new viewing experience takes a page from NFL RedZone, which has existed since 2009 and has become an essential channel for passionate pro football fans.

ESPN acquired rights to the RedZone brand in its deal with the NFL, which went into effect in January.

Keep up with all the latest in entertainment news

Subscribe to CableTV.com's email newsletter for the latest TV event viewing guides, entertaining takes, and money-saving promotions.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

Former tennis stars sound off on addition of RedZone

Patrick McEnroe and Mary Joe Fernandez have seen it all in professional tennis, whether as players or analysts. But they’re excited about what the new RedZone experience can mean for tennis fandom moving forward.

“RedZone to me is going to be amazing,” McEnroe said during a conference call with reporters in advance of the tournament. “I think that’s going to be super fun for the fan.”

Fernandez still loves watching matches in their entirety. But she knows that preference is becoming rarer, particularly among younger people with notoriously lower attention spans.

“ don’t always want to see a match from start to finish,” Fernandez said. “But to be able to go to the big points and the big moments, I think that’s fantastic.”

Does RedZone mark the future of watching tennis?

I’m more like Fernandez — if I’m watching tennis, I wanna be there for the whole thing. I was on the edge of my leather recliner for all five hours and 29 minutes of Carlos Alcaraz’s epic five-set comeback over Jannik Sinner in 2025 at the French Open.

Also like Fernandez, I like watching as much tennis as I can. I just don’t have that kind of time. So, for a fan like me, “RedZone at the U.S. Open” sounds very attractive. And I’d imagine it’s a good entry point for fans just getting into the sport, too.

McEnroe said the sport needs to attract younger viewers, and hopes RedZone could be part of that.

“They want to see lots of stuff,” McEnroe said of younger fans. “They want to get a lot of information. I think they also want the ability to communicate, put in their comments maybe up like they do on YouTube when you do a stream, something like that. I’m hoping we can try some of that stuff with RedZone.”

Fernandez echoed McEnroe’s point of attracting younger viewers. She recalled spending time at her tennis club in Ohio and noticing the younger players watching the Cincinnati Open on their phones.

“Interactive for the young fans,” Fernandez said. “It’s great if you can make comments like Patrick said. But everything now has to be easy, right? Have to be able to find it fast, get to the highlight quickly. … I think that’s the future. We need to keep improving and keep making it accessible on all platforms.”

With ESPN carrying three of the four tennis majors — TNT Sports has Wimbledon — the network has a large testing ground for its version RedZone. Maybe the name will change in the future to something more related to tennis rather than the last 20 yards of a football field.

“I think RedZone is a major step forward for us,” McEnroe said.

item.title: ESPN Unlimited Will Get Its First Price Increase, Alongside ESPN Select and Disney Bundle
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: ESPN is usually a great deal: a whole bundle of live sports coverage for the price of a streaming service. But it’s about to get a little more expensive.
item.content:encoded:
ESPN prices go up on September 17

Just about a year ago, ESPN overhauled its existing subscription system. ESPN+ became ESPN Select, and the streamer introduced a new tier called ESPN Unlimited for sports fans seeking the full ESPN experience. But now it’s time for ESPN’s yearly price increase. And both plans are getting in on the fun. ESPN Select’s new price is $13.99/mo., and ESPN Unlimited’s new price is $31.99/mo. Both changes will go into effect for current subscribers on September 17, 2026. Keep reading for more info on the upcoming increase!

Keep up with all the latest in entertainment news

Subscribe to CableTV.com's email newsletter for the latest TV event viewing guides, entertaining takes, and money-saving promotions.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

ESPN prices: then vs. now

The new ESPN prices are already live for new customers. But if you already subscribed to an ESPN plan before August 20, 2026, you’ll see the new prices on your first bill after September 17, 2026. Here’s what you can expect:

ESPN monthly prices

New price Old price ESPN+ content ESPN channels
ESPN Select $13.99/mo. $12.99/mo. ✔ —
ESPN Unlimited $31.99/mo. $29.99/mo. ✔ ✔

ESPN annual prices

New price Old price ESPN+ content ESPN channels
ESPN Select $139.99/yr. $129.99/yr. ✔ —
ESPN Unlimited $319.99/yr. $299.99/yr. ✔ ✔
Both of ESPN’s annual prices are also getting a price hike. But it’s not an unreasonable one. They follow the same rule of thumb as most streaming services’ annual plans: the same as ten payments of the monthly price. The Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Unlimited bundle will be staying the same amid the price changes, but the Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Select bundle will also be increasing by $2–$3/mo. depending on the plan. The other parts of the Disney Bundle — Disney+ and Hulu — will likely get their own price increase this October, if Disney follows its own trends. So keep an eye out, and we’ll report when the next streaming service gets a price hike. It’s probably coming sooner than you think.

item.title: Li’l Death: Where to Watch ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Wondering where to watch Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma? Our experts track theater showtimes, VOD dates, streaming news & Jane Schoenbrun’s films!
item.content:encoded:
The CableTV.com take

  • Jane Schoenbrun’s slasher film “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is in theaters now. You can buy tickets here.
  • “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” will eventually hit video-on-demand (VOD) retailers.
  • “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” isn’t on a subscription streaming service yet, but could eventually land on HBO Max™

While we’ve all been obsessed with “Obsession” and stuck on (er, in) “Backrooms,” a sneaky new slasher film snuck up behind us: Jane Schoenbrun’s bloody buzzy “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.”

The film stars Hannah Einbender (“Hacks”) as Kris Williams, a budding queer filmmaker who’s landed a gig directing the next film in the “Camp Miasma” slasher series. Kris decides they absolutely must cast Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the original film’s final girl, and sparks fly between the two — while blood sloshes all around them.

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” has already thrilled the festival circuit as well as moviegoers in select cities for the past couple of weeks. On Friday, Aug. 21, it will finally get a wide theatrical release. The film currently holds the highest rating of any 2026 horror film — even “Obsession” — on Rotten Tomatoes: 95% based on 197 critics’ reviews.

Here’s everything you need to know to watch “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” as well as Jane Schoenbrun’s other two acclaimed movies, “I Saw the TV Glow” and “We’re All Going to the World’s Fair.”

Looking for the hottest entertainment?

Subscribe to CableTV.com's email newsletter for the latest TV event viewing guides, entertaining takes, and money-saving promotions.

By signing up, you agree to our Privacy Policy & Terms and Conditions.

When will “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” be streaming?

Since “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is just barely getting a wide theatrical release, it could be anywhere from two to six weeks before the film is available to rent via video-on-demand (VOD) outlets.

It might be even longer before we see “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” hit a subscription streaming service. When that happens, it could be on HBO Max, which commonly streams Schoenbrun’s other two films (just not at the time of this writing). Since it’s spooky season, and “Camp Miasma” has tremendous hype behind it, I suspect we’ll see the film there by early October.

Where to watch “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma”

So, for now, the only way to watch “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is to go to the movies — you can buy tickets here.

Where to watch Jane Schoenbrun’s other movies

Although HBO Max has streamed Schoenbrun’s past films, they’re not on the service right now. You might find “We’re All Going to the World’s Fair” on The Criterion Channel, which has a free 7-day trial.

Otherwise, your best bets are to rent the films from video-on-demand (VOD) retailers like Apple TV, Fandango at Home, Plex, or Prime Video.

item.title: It’s Time for Peacock’s Annual Price Increase. Here’s What You Need to Know.

item.description: Peacock just applied its annual price increase to your subscription. How much do you have to pay now? Read on to find out.
item.content:encoded:
Peacock’s latest price increase hit this week

If you’ve been looking to sign up for Peacock this week, you might have noticed that the site prices differ from what third party guides and news sites claim. That’s because Peacock just raised its prices for new members, effective August 18. 2026. Existing customers will see this price increase on their next bill on or after September 17, 2026. So how much more will a Peacock subscription cost you, and is it worth it? Let’s dive into the details and find out.

How much does Peacock cost in 2026?

After the August 2026 price increase, a Peacock subscription will cost you anywhere between $8.99/mo. and $19.99/mo.

New price Old price Full Peacock library Ad-free? Live NBC?

Peacock Premium $12.99/mo. $10.99/mo. ✔ — —

Peacock’s lowest tier, Peacock Select, is going up by $1/mo. Its middle tier, Peacock Premium, is going up by $2/mo. And its highest tier, the ad-free Peacock Premium Plus, is going up by $3/mo. Peacock Premium Plus $199.99/yr. $169.99/yr. ✔ ✔ ✔
So is this new price increase reasonable? Peacock’s last price increase took effect in July 2025, which seems like just yesterday. But these days, most streaming services do raise their prices every year. It’s an unfortunate reality of the industry. Still, a three-dollar price increase on the only ad-free plan is pretty drastic — especially since it rose the same amount last year. It’s hard to believe that the Premium Plus plan has doubled in price (from $9.99/mo. to $19.99/mo.) since 2022. Peacock Premium is still the best way to get the streaming service (unless you can get a deal through another bundle or cable provider). Peacock Select’s price may be tempting, but its library is extremely limited compared to the pricier plans. Peacock Select customers lose out on live sports, movies, and Peacock Originals. Unfortunately, picking the best Peacock plan may mean you have to put up with ads. Unless you’re okay with that new, shocking price tag.

Peacock

Peacock has come a long way from the free service it was when it debuted back in 2020. It’s a pretty pricey option now, but we generally feel that it has the content to back it up — especially for sports fans.

Who we are

At CableTV.com, we’re not just entertainment experts — we’re also fans just like you. So while our first priority is reporting the best and most accurate information about TV providers and streaming services, we also love talking about our favorite shows and movies. So you can count on us to share our honest opinions and unbridled enthusiasm. For more on our process, check out our Editorial Policy.

item.title: Every Netflix, HBO Max, and Hulu Price Increase: The History of Streaming Service Prices
item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: I’ve compiled data on all of our favorite streaming services to see the bigger picture. Which services are making reasonable changes, and which are taking advantage of economic panic?
item.content:encoded:
It’s not just you; streaming prices are rising, fast

Almost every major streaming service has increased its prices several times in the last few years. It’s gotten to the point where yearly price hikes feel like the norm, but it’s easy to forget that it wasn’t always like this. Streaming used to be a cheap, dependable form of entertainment. Prices would stay steady for years at a time. But those days are over. We love streaming television here at CableTV.com, but we also want to hold entertainment platforms and conglomerates accountable. So I’ve compiled data on all of our favorite streaming services to see the bigger picture. Which streaming price increases are reasonable changes, and which are taking advantage of economic panic? Let’s find out.

Why trust us? Despite our company name, we love television in all its forms. (Cable-and-streaming-TV-dot-com just wouldn’t have the same ring.) Our entertainment experts have spent thousands of hours testing all of the best (and worst) streaming services, and hundreds more hours tracking and researching industry trends. It’s our job to keep an eye on everything the big corporate streamers get up to—so you can focus on enjoying your favorite shows.
Jump to:

Netflix pricing history

Netflix’s latest price increase went into effect in March 2026. Netflix currently offers three plans:

  • Netflix Standard with Ads ($8.99/mo., 2 streams)
  • Netflix Standard ($19.99/mo., 2 streams, no ads)
  • Netflix Premium ($26.99/mo., 4 streams, no ads)

Netflix broke its streaming service off from its DVD rental service in 2011 and stopped renting out DVDs altogether in 2023. Netflix Basic (1 stream) was discontinued in January 2025. All Netflix plans now provide at least two simultaneous streams.

Read More About Netflix

Netflix’s monthly price history

Netflix Basic Netflix Standard with Ads Netflix Standard Netflix Premium
2011 — — $7.99 —
2012 — — $7.99 —
2013 $6.99 — $7.99 $11.99
2014 $7.99 — $8.99 $11.99
2015 $7.99 — $9.99 $11.99
2016 $7.99 — $9.99 $11.99
2017 $8.99 — $10.99 $13.99
2018 $8.99 — $10.99 $13.99
2019 $8.99 — $12.99 $15.99
2020 $8.99 — $13.99 $17.99
2021 $8.99 — $13.99 $17.99
2022 $9.99 — $15.49 $19.99
2023 $11.99 $6.99 $15.49 $22.99
2024 $11.99 $6.99 $15.49 $22.99
2025 — $7.99 $17.99 $24.99
2026 — $8.99 $19.99 $26.99
Netflix’s streaming service began as a free perk for its DVD rental subscribers in 2007, but became a standalone option in 2011. Users could pay $7.99/mo. for Netflix’s full, ad-free library of television and movies. That price for a Standard subscription—that is, two streams and no ads—has steadily increased every few years since its inception. Netflix subscribers now have to make a choice: Pay over double what the original Netflix subscription cost to maintain their ad-free experience, or downgrade to Netflix Standard with Ads for a reasonable $8.99/mo. price tag. Of course, you could always upgrade to Netflix Premium for those coveted four streams. But $26.99/mo. is a lot, even considering inflation, and those four streams don’t guarantee you can share your password with anyone outside of your main household. That’s the hidden fee behind every Netflix subscription: Restricted password sharing. Standard subscribers can purchase one extra member for $6.99–$8.99/mo., and Premium subscribers can purchase two. Got more family members than that? You’re on your own.

Disney+ pricing history

Disney+’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. Disney+ currently offers two plans:

  • Disney+ Basic ($11.99/mo., 4 streams)
  • Disney+ Premium ($18.99/mo., 4 streams, no ads)

Read More About Disney+

Disney+’s monthly price history

Disney+ Basic Disney+ Premium
2019 — $6.99
2020 — $6.99
2021 — $7.99
2022 $7.99 $10.99
2023 $7.99 $13.99
2024 $9.99 $15.99
2025 $11.99 $18.99
2026 $11.99 $18.99
Disney+ launched in 2019 as an ad-free service, but introduced ads in 2022. Subscribers could choose to remove ads, but it would cost $3 more per month. Disney+’s price has risen astronomically since its inception. Where Netflix took about 14 years to double the price of its original plan, Disney+ did the same in just four. Rather than the steady increase over time to mirror inflation, it gives the impression that Disney is scrambling to recover costs (since cancelling and removing a bunch of shows didn’t seem to work). When I recommend Disney+, I’m not usually recommending the standalone streaming service. It just seems like too much money for too little content (unless you’re really passionate about Star Wars). Instead, it’s a much better deal to bundle Disney+ with Disney’s other major streaming service, Hulu. Later in 2026, this will be your only option to watch Hulu content, anyway (keep reading for more on that).

Hulu pricing history

Hulu’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. Hulu currently offers two (on-demand) plans:

  • Hulu Basic ($11.99/mo., 2 streams)
  • Hulu Premium ($18.99/mo., 2 streams, no ads)

Read More About Hulu

Hulu’s monthly price history

Hulu Basic Hulu Premium
2010 $7.99 —
2011 $7.99 —
2012 $7.99 —
2013 $7.99 —
2014 $7.99 —
2015 $7.99 $11.99
2016 $7.99 $11.99
2017 $7.99 $11.99
2018 $7.99 $11.99
2019 $5.99 $11.99
2020 $5.99 $11.99
2021 $6.99 $12.99
2022 $7.99 $14.99
2023 $7.99 $17.99
2024 $9.99 $18.99
2025 $11.99 $18.99
2026 $11.99 $18.99
Hulu was pretty chill about price increases for a long time. For its first eight years of existence, its plans stayed exactly the same. And since Hulu began as an ad-supported service rather than an ad-free one, the introduction of different price tiers didn’t feel like a total betrayal. But then Disney bought a majority stake in Hulu in 2019 and finished acquiring the service entirely in 2023. Since then, standalone prices—especially for Hulu Premium— have steadily increased, likely as an incentive to make users switch over to the Disney Bundle. In early 2025, I predicted that Disney would shut down Hulu as a standalone app and permanently merge it with Disney+. And guess what? I was right! You can expect the price of Disney+ to go up dramatically in late 2026 (likely in October) as they make the move official.

The Disney Bundle pricing history

The Disney Bundle’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. There are currently several ways to get The Disney Bundle. Here are the ones we’re tracking:

  • Duo Basic ($12.99/mo., Hulu and Disney+)
  • Duo Premium ($19.99/mo., Hulu and Disney+, no ads)
  • Trio Basic ($19.99/mo., Hulu, Disney+, and ESPN Select)
  • Trio Premium ($29.99/mo., Hulu, Disney+, and ESPN Select, no ads)

The Legacy Disney Bundle ($24.99/mo., Hulu, Disney+, and ESPN Select, no ads on Disney+) is only available to existing subscribers.

Read More About The Disney Bundle

The Disney Bundle’s monthly price history

Legacy Disney Bundle Duo Basic Duo Premium Trio Basic Trio Premium
2019 $12.99 — — — —
2020 $12.99 — — — —
2021 $13.99 — — — —
2022 $14.99 $9.99 — $12.99 $19.99
2023 $18.99 $9.99 $19.99 $14.99 $24.99
2024 $21.99 $10.99 $19.99 $16.99 $26.99
2025 $24.99 $12.99 $19.99 $19.99 $29.99
2026 $24.99 $12.99 $19.99 $19.99 $29.99
The Disney Bundle is a great way to get multiple streaming services for cheap—if you’re okay with ads. The Duo Premium and Trio Premium plans are pretty pricey in their own right, even if they’re technically better deals than subscribing to every service individually. In my opinion, the gap between the Basic and Premium prices is way too high. Disney Bundle subscribers can also now access Hulu through Disney+’s interface. You can expect to see more changes in (likely October) 2026 when Disney finally shuts down Hulu as a standalone app and makes the Disney Bundle its biggest priority.

HBO Max pricing history

Max’s latest price increase went into effect in October 2025. Max currently offers three plans:

  • HBO Max Basic with Ads ($10.99/mo., 2 streams)
  • HBO Max Standard ($18.49/mo., 2 streams, no ads)
  • HBO Max Premium ($22.99/mo., 4 streams, no ads)

HBO Max changed its name to Max in 2023 and changed it back to HBO Max in Summer 2025.

Read More About HBO Max

HBO Max’s monthly price history

HBO Max Basic with Ads HBO Max Standard HBO Max Premium
2020 — $14.99 —
2021 $9.99 $14.99 —
2022 $9.99 $14.99 —
2023 $9.99 $15.99 $19.99
2024 $9.99 $16.99 $20.99
2025 $10.99 $18.49 $22.99
2026 $10.99 $18.49 $22.99
When HBO Max launched in 2020, it was already pretty expensive. That’s because it couldn’t be cheaper than the HBO cable channel, a premium add-on with a premium price tag, or its streaming predecessor, HBO Now, which only streamed HBO content. So unlike Disney+ and Peacock, HBO Max never had the chance to market itself as the cool, cheap, cable alternative. Instead, it began as a way for non-cable subscribers to watch WarnerMedia-owned content on demand. The “HBO” brand name promised high-quality, prestige entertainment and was bolstered by a library full of titles from all of WarnerMedia’s brands: DC, Turner Classic Movies, Cartoon Network, Adult Swim, Studio Ghibli, and more. But things went downhill after WarnerMedia merged with Discovery to form Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD). The two media giants’ streaming services, HBO Max and Discovery+, merged into the monosyllabic “Max.” Max lost its premium cable identity when it lost its HBO branding, and the platform was flooded with Discovery’s most popular reality shows. (Discovery+ continues to this day as a standalone service that features dozens of additional reality TV franchises and spinoffs.) Something really bothers me about the name change—WBD justified it with the claim that the HBO branding was scaring parents away. WBD wanted to welcome kids onto their platform. This should have been a slam dunk because WBD owns Cartoon Network. But instead of investing in animation and kids’ content, Max slowly removed popular CN titles from its library. WBD reduced spending on animation, shut down CN’s physical headquarters, and stripped away the station’s identity. Kids lost interest in Max. In 2025, WBD gave up on kids. It sold off “Sesame Street” to Netflix and “The Amazing World of Gumball” to Hulu, put the “HBO” back in “HBO Max,” and is desperately trying to claw back its standing as the place to find serious adult television.

Amazon Prime Video pricing history

Prime Video’s latest price increase went into effect in April 2026. You can choose to subscribe to Amazon Prime Video on its own:

  • Amazon Prime Video ($8.99/mo., 3 streams)

Or bundle it with a full Amazon Prime membership:

  • Amazon Prime ($14.99/mo., 3 streams)

Prime Video was ad-free until January 2024, when it put ads on most of its content. Amazon Prime Ultra is an add-on that costs $4.99/mo., and removes ads from most Prime content.

Read More About Prime Video

Amazon Prime Video’s monthly price history

Amazon Prime Video (ads) Amazon Prime Video (no ads) Amazon Prime (ads) Amazon Prime (no ads)
2016 — $8.99 — $10.99
2017 — $8.99 — $10.99
2018 — $8.99 — $12.99
2019 — $8.99 — $12.99
2020 — $8.99 — $12.99
2021 — $8.99 — $12.99
2022 — $8.99 — $14.99
2023 — $8.99 — $14.99
2024 $8.99 $11.98 $14.99 $17.98
2025 $8.99 $11.98 $14.99 $17.98
2026 $8.99 $13.98 $14.99 $19.98
Amazon Prime Video’s pricing structure was pretty reasonable until 2024. Customers could access the service either by subscribing to the full Amazon Prime membership (for free two-day shipping and more) or by subscribing to Prime Video as a standalone service. But Amazon ruffled a lot of feathers in 2024 by putting ads on all of its content, not just the titles it inherited from the now-defunct free ad-supported television (FAST) service Freevee. If customers hate the frequent interruptions, they can remove them with Amazon Prime Video Ultra, which is an additional $4.99/mo. fee on top of the regular subscription. Even though Amazon doesn’t advertise it this way, I consider this to be a new pricing tier, so I’ve written it up in the table above accordingly. Prime Video took a page out of Disney+’s playbook: get customers hooked on ad-free television and then take it away, hiding the privilege behind another paywall. It’s a transparent attempt to wring more money out of customers, and I’m not a fan.

Apple TV pricing history

Apple TV’s latest price increase went into effect in August 2025. Apple TV currently offers one plan:

  • Apple TV ($12.99/mo., 6 streams, no ads)

Read More About Apple TV+

Apple TV’s monthly price history

Apple TV
2019 $4.99
2020 $4.99
2021 $4.99
2022 $6.99
2023 $9.99
2024 $9.99
2025 $12.99
2026 $12.99
Apple TV’s price history is easy to track because it’s only ever offered one plan. And that plan has only gone up in price three times in the platform’s history. It’s surprising that Apple TV has never imitated the multiple-tier-cash-grabs of its competitors, but that’s why I always rate the service so highly. I find a lot of other streaming services’ pricing schemes to be anti-consumer. I’m hesitant to praise Apple TV too much for keeping its plans cheap and simple. Soon after I praised Prime Video for doing the same in 2023, Amazon decided to charge customers an extra $2.99/mo. for the same ad-free service they’d always gotten. And then there’s the whole debacle of its 2025 rebrand from “Apple TV+” to “Apple TV.” But Apple TV’s content library is almost entirely original. Maybe the lack of licensing fees will keep prices low (and advertising far, far away) for a little while longer.

Paramount+ pricing history

Paramount+’s latest price increase went into effect in January 2026. Paramount+ currently offers two plans:

  • Paramount+ Essential ($8.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • Paramount+ Premium ($13.99/mo., 3 streams, no ads)

Paramount+ Premium was discontinued in 2023 when it was replaced by the newly discounted Paramount+ with SHOWTIME bundle. The Paramount+ with SHOWTIME bundle was then renamed to Paramount+ Premium in 2025.

Read More About Paramount+

Paramount+’s monthly price history

Paramount+ Essential Paramount+ Premium Paramount+ with SHOWTIME
2021 $4.99 $9.99 —
2022 $4.99 $9.99 $14.99
2023 $5.99 — $11.99
2024 $7.99 — $12.99
2025 $7.99 $12.99 $12.99
2026 $8.99 $13.99 —
Paramount+ is an interesting case because its premium tier offers two streaming services in one. Unlike other streaming bundles, you can’t subscribe to both components of Paramount+ with SHOWTIME separately. SHOWTIME no longer exists as its own entity, and even the premium cable channel is called Paramount+ with SHOWTIME now. Paramount+ with SHOWTIME is cheaper now than when the bundle first debuted in 2022. In a remarkably reasonable decision, the company split the difference between the $14.99/mo. bundle price and the $9.99/mo. price of the Premium plan it was replacing. It’s rare to see a streaming service decrease the price of one of its plans over time—especially without taking something important away. The only other instance that comes to mind is when Hulu decreased its prices in 2019 in an attempt to pull customers away from its notoriously expensive competitor, Netflix. And because nothing can be simple with Paramount+: the Paramount+ with SHOWTIME tier is now called Paramount+ Premium. But it’s not the same Paramount+ Premium that the company offered in 2022; this time, it comes with SHOWTIME content. It’s just not in the name anymore. Forget SHOWTIME exists, actually. That branding is so 2024.

Peacock pricing history

Peacock’s latest price increase went into effect in August 2026. Peacock currently offers three plans:

  • Peacock Select ($8.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • Peacock Premium ($12.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • Peacock Premium Plus ($19.99/mo., 3 streams, no ads)

Peacock discontinued its free tier in 2023.

Read More About Peacock

Peacock’s monthly price history

Peacock Select Peacock Premium Peacock Premium Plus
2020 — $4.99 $9.99
2021 — $4.99 $9.99
2022 — $4.99 $9.99
2023 — $5.99 $11.99
2024 — $7.99 $13.99
2025 $7.99 $10.99 $16.99
2026 $8.99 $12.99 $19.99
Peacock’s plan names have never made too much sense. Most streaming services use “Premium” to mean “ad-free,” but not Peacock. At Peacock, the only way you’re getting rid of ads is by subscribing to Premium Plus. This whole naming scheme is probably because Peacock used to offer a free tier when it was first starting out, but it was discontinued in 2023. Nowadays, instead of a free tier, the thriftiest Peacock plan is called Peacock Select. Like Premium, it has ads, but it doesn’t allow access to a lot of Peacock’s library. You’ll miss out on originals, sports, and movies—Peacock’s three biggest strengths. But you can still enjoy old episodes of “The Office,” I guess.

ESPN pricing history

ESPN’s latest price increase went into effect in August 2025. ESPN currently offers two plans:

  • ESPN Select ($11.99/mo., 3 streams)
  • ESPN Unlimited ($29.99/mo., 3 streams)

ESPN  subscriptions are only available with ads. ESPN Select is the new name of ESPN+, and ESPN Unlimited is a new plan introduced in 2025.

Read More About ESPN+

ESPN+’s monthly price history

ESPN Select ESPN Unlimited
2018 $4.99 —
2019 $4.99 —
2020 $5.99 —
2021 $6.99 —
2022 $9.99 —
2023 $10.99 —
2024 $11.99 —
2025 $11.99 $29.99
2026 $11.99 $29.99
Unlike my colleague Taylor Kujawa, I’m not much of a sports fan beyond the occasional baseball game, so ESPN+’s new subscription system was initially pretty confusing to me. Essentially, the ESPN+ streaming service still exists, it’s just been rebranded as ESPN Select. Superfans can upgrade to the $29.99/mo. ESPN Unlimited plan for even more sports content, like the ESPN, ESPN2, and ESPNU cable channels. Previously, ESPN+ did not include everything airing on ESPN the cable channel. “For customers, ESPN’s unlimited direct-to-consumer service is a double-edged sword,” says CableTV.com Sports Editor Taylor Kujawa. “It’s perfect for fans of the ESPN brand and the sports covered under ESPN’s media agreements. But the rise of these standalone streaming services could make watching sports much more expensive than it already is.” Both of theses new plans are part of a larger service called simply “ESPN,” not to be confused with the ESPN cable channel.

Crunchyroll pricing history

Crunchyroll’s latest price increase went into effect in January 2026. Crunchyroll currently offers three paid tiers:

  • Crunchyroll Fan ($9.99/mo., 1 stream)
  • Crunchyroll Mega Fan ($13.99/mo., 4 streams, game vault)
  • Crunchyroll Ultimate Fan ($17.99/mo., 6 streams, game vault, manga)

Crunchyroll discontinued its free tier at the end of 2025.

Read More About Crunchyroll

Crunchyroll’s monthly price history

Crunchyroll Fan Crunchyroll Mega Fan Crunchyroll Ultimate Fan
2009 $6.95 —
2010 $6.95 — —
2011 $6.95 — —
2012 $6.95 — —
2013 $6.95 — —
2014 $6.95 — —
2015 $6.95 — —
2016 $6.95 — —
2017 $6.95 — —
2018 $6.95 — —
2019 $6.95 — —
2020 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2021 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2022 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2023 $7.99 $9.99 $14.99
2024 $7.99 $11.99 $15.99
2025 $7.99 $11.99 $15.99
2026 $9.99 $13.99 $17.99
Crunchyroll began as a free service in 2006, and initially, memberships were more of a donation thing to keep the site running. Users would pay for higher-quality streaming and the privilege of a star-shaped badge. Crunchyroll started formally offering a premium membership by 2009. This predates Netflix’s streaming service; there was no blueprint for how these subscriptions should work. In addition to the standard credit card and PayPal payment methods, users could also pay for their memberships by physically putting a check in an envelope and sending it through the mail. It was a different era. Early Crunchyroll memberships would give members same-day simulcasts and access to 100% of Crunchyroll’s library. Free users would get simulcasts a week late, and access to “most” of Crunchyroll’s library. It’s hard to say exactly how much “most” is, and how that percentage has changed over time. Unlike today, there weren’t a lot of online news articles documenting streaming service policy changes in 2009. I’m getting a lot of my info by crawling through janky captures on the Internet Archive.Over the past several years, Crunchyroll put more and more of its content behind a paywall until it finally discontinued the free subscription entirely at the end of 2025. As of January 2026, if you want to watch anything on Crunchyroll, you’ll need a paid account, just like any other streaming service. When you compare Crunchyroll to other streaming services, you realize it’s actually still a pretty good deal. None of its paid tiers have ads, and you get the full anime experience for a relatively low price. The higher tiers are just nice-to-haves, with bonus perks like video games and manga. Crunchyroll’s subscriber count has been booming in recent years, so this paywall strategy seems to be working for them. But it’s still disappointing to see something that used to be free jump up to ten dollars a month.

How did we get here?

Here at CableTV.com, we’ve been helping TV lovers make smart choices since 2007. We believe that you should spend your time enjoying the best entertainment, not poring over twenty years of news articles to figure out if you’re getting a good deal or not. That’s where we come in. Our staff of TV experts spends every day scouring the web for information on streaming services past, present, and future so you can focus on the things that matter. Like bingeing another season of The White Lotus. For more on our process, check out How We Rank.

item.dc:creator: CableTV.com
item.description: Disney’s biggest promotional event, D23, has come and gone. Check out our recap for all of the biggest announcements from 2026.
item.content:encoded:
A weekend full of Disney headlines

Disney dazzled audiences this weekend with its Disney Entertainment Showcase at D23, its annual convention. For those lucky enough to be in the Honda Center, they were treated to musical numbers and sneak peaks from all sorts of upcoming Disney properties. The rest of us will have to wait until the movies come out in 2027, 2028, and beyond…. But we can still enjoy certain teasers and clips from the show. I’ve compiled a roundup of what I consider the biggest news to come out of D23 this year. Ready? Let’s get started!

“The Bluey Movie”

At long last, “The Bluey Movie” has a teaser trailer. The film, inspired by the super-popular kids’ show, was first announced in 2024. We don’t know a ton about the movie’s plot, but the teaser trailer shows off a brand new 3D art style for the little blue dog and her sister. The movie will come to theaters on August 6, 2027, and will likely appear on Disney+ several months after that. Oh, and don’t worry Australians — you’ll be able to stream it as well.

Good news for “Kingdom Hearts” fans

I spend a lot of time researching upcoming animated series, and this is one I’m super excited for. “Kingdom Hearts” is a popular video game series that mixes “Final Fantasy” with iconic Disney characters like Donald, Mickey, and Goofy. Since the Disney mobile game “Twisted Wonderland” got an anime adaptation last year, it was only a matter of time before “Kingdom Hearts” got its own show, too. The “Kingdom Hearts” show will premiere on Disney Channel and Disney+, but does not yet have a release date.And that’s not the only “Kingdom Hearts” news to come out of D23 this year. “Kingdom Hearts IV” got a new trailer, featuring a look at the game’s new “Coco”-inspired world. “Kingdom Hearts IV” will come to Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S in late 2027.

New Pixar films

Do you like sequels? Disney’s got sequels. We got a first look at two new Pixar sequels this D23: “Incredibles 3” and “Coco 2.” “Incredibles 3” will focus on the Parr kids: Violet, Jack-Jack, and Dash. This time, the siblings will be taking on a new and powerful supervillain. It doesn’t seem like they’ve aged that much in the last 22 years, which isn’t much of a surprise since executive producer Brad Bird has said that it’s important to him that the trio remain children. “Incredibles 3” will come to theaters on June 16, 2028. Miguel, on the other hand, has aged. The new “Coco 2” concept art shows Miguel as a teenager, and his would-be grandfather Ernesto de la Cruz as a more bedraggled, menacing version of himself. “Coco 2” will come to theaters in November 2029.And if sequels aren’t your thing, you can still look forward to the upcoming, original Pixar film, “Ghost Market.” It’s Pixar’s first horror film, but it’s “not like some of those other scary movies.” The first teaser trailer, which you can watch above, shows a ghost enjoying a bowl of ramen. And now I’m hungry. “Ghost Market” will come to theaters in Spring 2028.

Disney Princesses are back in the spotlight

Disney Princesses are having a moment right now. If you didn’t know, World Princess Week began on August 16, and will run until August 22. Disney+ is celebrating with a wave of new content, including a filmed concert featuring Disney Princesses past and present.But as for Disney Princesses of the future? Fans can look forward to “Frozen 3,” which was heavily promoted at this year’s conference. Attendees saw an exclusive clip from the film, showing Elsa pulling Anna away from her and Kristoff’s wedding to investigate a mysterious new ice queen. And some of the actors made an appearance to sing new songs from the film. “Frozen 3” will come to theaters in Fall 2027.Meanwhile, on the live-action side of things, fans were treated to a video message from Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim, stars of the new live-action “Tangled” film. They’re filming in Spain right now, so the message showed them in full costume travelling around the real Spanish buildings Disney is using to represent the kingdom of Corona. “Tangled” will come to theaters on March 31, 2028.
